q: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃?
x: M(NH₄NO₃) = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80 g mol⁻¹, and it contains two N atoms: 28/80 × 100 = 35%. Counting only the ammonium nitrogen gives 17.5%, and 46.7% is the value for urea.

q: In the manufacture of urea, ammonia and carbon dioxide first combine under high pressure to form an intermediate, which then loses water. The intermediate is:
x: 2NH₃ + CO₂ → NH₂COONH₄, then NH₂COONH₄ → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O on heating. Ammonium carbonate and hydrogencarbonate would also need water as a reactant and are not the urea intermediate.

q: Urea is made by the overall reaction 2NH₃ + CO₂ → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O. What mass of urea can be made from 34 kg of ammonia?
x: 34 kg NH₃ is 2 kmol, which gives 1 kmol urea; M(CO(NH₂)₂) = 12 + 16 + 28 + 4 = 60 g mol⁻¹, so 60 kg. Using a 1 : 1 mole ratio gives 120 kg.

q: Which element is a micronutrient for plants?
x: N, P and K are the primary macronutrients, needed in large amounts and supplied by NPK fertilisers. Zinc is needed only in traces, so it is a micronutrient.

q: In modern fertiliser plants, the nitric acid used to make ammonium nitrate is produced by:
o: Heating sodium nitrate with concentrated H₂SO₄
Catalytic oxidation of ammonia with air over platinum
x: In the Ostwald process 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O over Pt; NO is oxidised to NO₂ and absorbed in water to give HNO₃, which is then neutralised: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. NaNO₃ with H₂SO₄ is a laboratory method, and the contact process makes H₂SO₄.

q: Rock phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, is treated with sulphuric acid to make superphosphate of lime. The purpose is to:
o: Remove all the calcium as CaCO₃
Reduce the phosphate to elemental phosphorus
Convert the insoluble phosphate into water-soluble Ca(H₂PO₄)₂
x: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ + 2CaSO₄. Plants cannot take up insoluble Ca₃(PO₄)₂, but calcium dihydrogenphosphate dissolves in soil water; the CaSO₄ stays mixed in the product.

q: A field needs 28 kg of nitrogen. What mass of ammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄ (132 g mol⁻¹), supplies exactly this amount?
x: 28 kg N is 2 kmol N atoms. Each (NH₄)₂SO₄ contains 2 N, so 1 kmol = 132 kg is needed. Taking one N per formula unit gives 264 kg, and 60 kg is the mass of urea that would supply the same nitrogen.

q: The two main raw materials for Portland cement are:
x: Limestone supplies CaO, and clay supplies SiO₂, Al₂O₃ and Fe₂O₃. Gypsum is added only at the end, when the clinker is ground.

q: A small amount of gypsum is ground with cement clinker. Its purpose is to:
o: Slow down the setting of the cement
Speed up the setting of the cement
Supply the silica needed for strength
Act as a fuel in the kiln
x: Without gypsum, the calcium aluminates in clinker react with water almost at once (flash set). Gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, retards setting and gives time to work the cement. Thinking it speeds up setting is the common slip.

q: The oxide present in the largest proportion by mass in Portland cement is:
x: Portland cement is roughly 60–67% CaO, 17–25% SiO₂, 3–8% Al₂O₃ and smaller amounts of Fe₂O₃. Silica comes second, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

q: A cement raw mix contains 80% CaCO₃ by mass. What mass of CO₂ is released from the CaCO₃ when 500 kg of the mix is heated in the kiln?
x: CaCO₃ = 0.80 × 500 = 400 kg = 4 kmol; CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ gives 4 kmol CO₂ = 4 × 44 = 176 kg. Treating all 500 kg as CaCO₃ gives 220 kg.

q: In the kraft (sulphate) process for making paper pulp, wood chips are cooked with:
x: The kraft process uses a hot solution of NaOH and Na₂S, which dissolves the lignin and frees the cellulose fibres. Calcium hydrogensulphite with SO₂ is the sulphite process, and chlorine is used later for bleaching.

q: The main aim of pulping wood in the paper industry is to:
o: Remove lignin and separate the cellulose fibres
x: Lignin binds the cellulose fibres together and turns paper yellow; pulping dissolves it, leaving cellulose fibres that are formed into sheets. Paper is made of cellulose, so removing it or hydrolysing it to glucose would leave nothing to make paper from.

q: The setting and hardening of cement after it is mixed with water is mainly due to:
o: Reaction of the cement with nitrogen in the air
Melting and re-solidifying of the clinker
Hydration of calcium silicates and aluminates
x: Water reacts with the calcium silicates and aluminates in an exothermic hydration, forming interlocking hydrated crystals and gels. The water is used up chemically, not simply evaporated.

q: Crude petroleum is separated into fractions such as petrol, kerosene and diesel by fractional distillation, which depends on differences in:
x: Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons that boil within a range; smaller molecules have lower boiling points and condense higher up the column. Density differs between fractions but is not the basis of the separation.

q: Dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, is cracked to give only octane, C₈H₁₈, and ethene. How many molecules of ethene form from one molecule of dodecane?
x: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄: carbon 12 = 8 + 4 and hydrogen 26 = 18 + 8. With only one ethene, two carbons and four hydrogens are left unaccounted for.

q: Standard enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): H₂ −286, CH₄ −890, C₂H₅OH −1368, C₈H₁₈ −5470. Which fuel releases the most energy per gram?
x: Per gram: H₂ 286 ÷ 2 = 143 kJ; CH₄ 890 ÷ 16 ≈ 56 kJ; C₂H₅OH 1368 ÷ 46 ≈ 30 kJ; C₈H₁₈ 5470 ÷ 114 ≈ 48 kJ. Octane releases the most per mole, which is the tempting slip.

q: Catalytic reforming in an oil refinery is used mainly to:
o: Break large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes
Separate crude oil into fractions by boiling point
Turn straight-chain alkanes into branched and aromatic hydrocarbons for better petrol
x: Reforming rearranges molecules (isomerisation, cyclisation, aromatisation) with little change in carbon number, raising the octane number of petrol. Breaking large molecules is cracking, and removing sulphur is hydrodesulphurisation.

q: Waste PVC should not be disposed of by open burning mainly because it releases:
o: HCl gas and toxic chlorinated dioxins
x: PVC, (–CH₂–CHCl–)ₙ, is about 57% chlorine by mass; burning it gives corrosive HCl and, in low-temperature fires, highly toxic dioxins. Polythene, with no chlorine, burns completely to CO₂ and water, and PVC contains no sulphur.

q: Standard enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C (coal) −394, CH₄ −890, C₂H₆ −1560, C₃H₈ −2220. Which fuel releases the most energy per mole of CO₂ produced?
x: Divide by the number of carbon atoms: C 394, CH₄ 890, C₂H₆ 780 and C₃H₈ 740 kJ per mol CO₂. Propane releases the most energy per mole of fuel, but methane gives the most energy for each mole of CO₂.
